paras: The bombing of Jesse Binga's office and the Robinson residence was a pair of bomb attacks on Black-occupied property on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, on a single night in March 1919, apparently Wednesday, March 19. Bombs thrown from a passing automobile wrecked the real estate and banking office of Jesse Binga, a Black banker, and damaged the Calumet avenue building where the family of Alex J. Robinson lived. No one was killed, and the Black press presented the attack as the latest in a series of bombings aimed at Black families moving into formerly white sections.

According to the St. Louis Argus, Black families had moved into previously white residential districts of the South Side after the start of the war, when Black laborers came from the South to work in munitions and packing plants. Binga was an agent for a number of South Side buildings and had been leasing apartments formerly occupied by white families to Black tenants. The Associated Negro Press (ANP) counted this as the third bomb on the South Side in three weeks and more than a dozen in the past year.

Shortly after 11 o'clock at night, a roadster passed 4724 South State street, a three-flat building with Binga's real estate, insurance and banking office on the first floor. A girl on the sidewalk saw one of two men in the car throw something into the hallway at the foot of the stairs, and the blast that followed wrecked Binga's office and broke windows on both sides of the street. A resident named Leary jumped in fright from a third-story window; he went to Provident hospital but was not seriously hurt.

Minutes later the car turned at Forty-first street, swerved to the curb in front of 4041 Calumet avenue and turned around, and a second bomb exploded. Windows were broken in almost every house in the block, and the Robinson family, who lived on the first floor, ran out in their night clothes. The ANP put the damage at thousands of dollars.

Police tried to trace the automobile, but the only description they had was that it carried no lights. The Chicago city council adopted resolutions, introduced by Aldermen Jackson and Anderson, calling for the most thorough investigation of the bombings. The ANP reported that indignation ran high and that people were asking "Where will it strike next?", while one citizen warned that the bombers would someday "throw at the wrong number." No report of an arrest appears in the coverage.

The first report found was a three-sentence Chicago wire dated March 21, printed by the Twin City Guardian on March 22 under "Bomb Wrecks Three Buildings," which said two Negro apartment houses and a Negro real estate office had been wrecked and no one injured. A week later the ANP story ran in the Baltimore Afro-American as "Another Bomb Outrage in Chicago," in the Cleveland Advocate as "Hoodlums Still Bomb Places of Race Folk in Chicago," and in the Dallas Express under a headline beginning "Infuriated Whites." That story stated that all the bombings had been traced "more or less" to whites incensed at the valuable property Black people were acquiring in exclusive sections of the South Side.

The St. Louis Argus printed a separately written and more detailed account on April 4 under "Bombs Destroy Negro Homes," with the eyewitness girl, the addresses and the injured man. Unlike the ANP version, the Argus also passed on a police statement that Binga had hired non-union workers, a suggestion of a labor motive that it did not pursue. It closed by noting the death of six-year-old Ernestine Ellis in an earlier explosion on Indiana avenue and the refusal of many Black families to leave their homes.

The reports differ on the date: the ANP copies, datelined March 25 or 27, said "Wednesday" or "this week," while the Argus said "one night of last week" and the matching wire was dated March 21, which points to March 19 rather than March 26. The ANP believed one person threw both bombs, whereas the Argus eyewitness saw two men in the car. The wire reported no injuries, while the Argus named Leary as slightly hurt.

reader.title: Bombing of Jesse Binga's office and the Robinson residence, Chicago (March 1919)
bases: Two bombs thrown from an automobile wrecked a Black banker's office and damaged a Black family's residence and apartment buildings, with no deaths (A2, A4, A9).

A brief March 21 wire (A2), the Associated Negro Press story (A3, A4) and the separately written St. Louis Argus account (A8, A9) agree on two bombs thrown from an automobile at Black-occupied South Side property including a real estate office.

accounts.label: Chicago wire
accounts.gist: Two Negro apartment houses and a Negro real estate office were wrecked by two bombs thrown from a speeding automobile; no one was injured.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press
accounts.gist: Two bombs on the same night, apparently thrown by one person from an automobile, hit Binga's branch banking offices and Robinson's residence; it was the third South Side bomb in three weeks and more than a dozen in a year, traced to whites angered by Black property buying.

accounts.label: St. Louis Argus correspondent
accounts.gist: A girl saw two men in a lightless roadster throw the first bomb into the hallway by Binga's office shortly after 11 p.m.; the car then bombed 4041 Calumet avenue; Leary was slightly hurt jumping from a window.

accounts.label: Police (as reported by the Argus)
accounts.gist: Police said Binga had hired a number of non-union workers ('jailors' in the OCR), implying a labor motive.

framing.detail: The Afro-American headlined 'Another Bomb Outrage in Chicago' and the Cleveland Advocate 'Hoodlums Still Bomb Places of Race Folk,' blaming whites incensed by Black property ownership.
The Dallas Express ran the ANP text under 'Infuriated Whites Resort...'.
The St. Louis Argus headlined 'Bombs Destroy Negro Homes' and set the bombing among Black families moving into white districts, but also printed the police suggestion of a non-union labor motive.
The Twin City Guardian ran a three-sentence wire, 'Bomb Wrecks Three Buildings,' with no motive.

conflicts.note: The ANP datelines vary between copies. The March 21 wire, matching in every detail, and the Argus's 'last week' place the bombing before March 21; the ANP 'Wednesday' then most likely means March 19, not March 26.

info: A night shortly before 21 March 1919: the ANP says 'on Wednesday in the night' (dateline March 27), the Argus 'one night of last week' (dateline March 27), and a Chicago wire dated March 21 already reported the blasts; the Wednesday before March 21 was 19 March.
South Side of Chicago: Jesse Binga's office at 4724 South State street and the building at 4041 Calumet avenue.

Jesse Binga, Black banker and real estate agent, whose office was wrecked; the family of Alex J. Robinson, on the first floor of 4041 Calumet avenue; Black residents of the two apartment buildings; a man named Leary, hurt when he jumped from a third-story window.
